# Regression

# Introduction : re-framing the target

In that part we will use all the algorithms we have seen previously but in the frame of a regression rather than a classification.

**The difference is that now our target vector (i.e. what we want to predict) is not a class (a discrete variable) but rather a number that can take a continuity of values.**

The algorithms are going to use very similar methods than the ones used in classification, **the main change is the loss function used to train your model and the scoring used to evaluate this model.**

**For classification** we saw two main types of **loss function**:

-   (log-)likelihood for models such as the logidsitc regression
-   GINI impurity, for trees

And plenty of **scoring systems**, but at least two in depth:

-   Accuracy
-   Area under the ROC curve.

In regression problems the loss functions and the scoring are metrics which you may already know.

The two main **loss functions** that you will minimize while training your model are :

-   Mean square error/ quadratic loss/ L2 loss **(MSE)** : $\frac{\Sigma^{n}_{i=1}(y_{i}-\hat{y}_{i})^{2}}{n}$
-   Mean absolute error/ L1 loss **(MAE)** : $\frac{\Sigma^{n}_{i=1}|y_{i}-\hat{y}_{i}|}{n}$

Where \* $n$ are the number of training examples \* $i$ the $i$-th training example in the data set \* $y_{i}$ the ground truth target value for that $i$-th example and \* $\hat{y_{i}}$ the estimated value of the target for the $i$-th example.

And the **scores**

-   value of the minimized loss function used (MSE or MAE)
-   **R squared** : $1-\frac{\Sigma^{n}_{i=1}(y_{i}-\hat{y}_{i})^{2}}{\Sigma^{n}_{i=1}(y_{i}-\bar{y}_{i})^{2}}$: the proportion of the target's variance that's explained by the model
-   **Adjusted R squared** : $1-(1-\frac{\Sigma^{n}_{i=1}(y_{i}-\hat{y}_{i})^{2}}{\Sigma^{n}_{i=1}(y_{i}-\bar{y}_{i})^{2}}\frac{n-1}{n-(k+1)})$ , with k the degree of freedom; similar to R-squared, but takes into account the number of variables in the model.
-   **Max error** : $max(|y_{i}-\hat{y}_{i}|)$
-   **Variance explained** : $1-\frac{Var(\{y_{i}-\bar{y}_{i}\}_{i})}{Var(\{y_{i}\}_{i})}$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

We will use a DNA methylation dataset from [Naue etal. 2017](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1872497317301643?via%3Dihub), as prepared for another [regression tutorial from the GTN](https://training.galaxyproject.org/training-material/topics/statistics/tutorials/regression_machinelearning/tutorial.html).

It consists in measurements of the methylation levels of 13 biomarkers to try to predict age.

The train and the test data have already been separated in two separate tables:

```{r}
df_meth = read.table( "https://zenodo.org/record/2545213/files/train_rows.csv",
                      sep= '\t', header = TRUE
                      )
df_meth %>% head()
```

```{r}
df_meth_test = read.table("https://zenodo.org/record/2545213/files/test_rows_labels.csv",
                          sep= '\t', header = TRUE)
df_meth_test %>% head()
```

```{r}
print( paste( "train rows:", df_meth %>% nrow() ))
print( paste( "test rows :", df_meth_test %>% nrow() ))

print( df_meth %>% colnames() )
```

# A little bit on data exploration for regression

let's check how the different features and the target interact with each others.

```{r}
cor_matrix = cor( df_meth, method = "pearson" )
palette <- colorRampPalette(c("blue","white","red"))(100)
pheatmap(cor_matrix,
         display_numbers = TRUE,
          color=palette, breaks=seq(-1,1,length.out=100))
```

We see that ELOVL2_6 has a very high correlation with age, the target. Perhaps a model with just this marker would be enough?

```{r}
ggplot(df_meth, aes( x = ELOVL2_6, y = Age )) + geom_point()
```

# Linear regression

We will start with a reduced dataset for visualization purposes.

```{r}
X_ELOVL2_6 = df_meth %>% select( Age , ELOVL2_6 ) %>%
    arrange(ELOVL2_6)
## to plot nice curves, it is interesting to get an ordered version of X
## points sorted by their values of ELOVL2_6

X_ELOVL2_6 %>% head()
```

Here, as we will build a simple linear model with a single feature, we actually have no hyper-parameter at this point.

So we can just build the model directly:

```{r}
model = linear_reg( engine = 'lm' ) %>%
    fit( Age ~ ELOVL2_6 , X_ELOVL2_6 )
X_ELOVL2_6_a = augment( model , X_ELOVL2_6 ) # adds predictions to X_ELOVL2

R2  = rsq(  X_ELOVL2_6_a , truth = Age , estimate = .pred )
RMSE= rmse( X_ELOVL2_6_a , truth = Age , estimate = .pred )

## plotting
ggplot( X_ELOVL2_6_a , aes( x = ELOVL2_6, y = Age )) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_line( aes( x = ELOVL2_6, y = .pred ) ) +
    ggtitle( paste( "simple linear regression - R^2=" , 
                    round(R2$.estimate,3) , " - RMSE=", round(RMSE$.estimate,2)  ) )

```

If we want to compute a cross-validated score for this simple model we can use:

```{r}
fit_resamples(
  object    = linear_reg( engine = 'lm' ),
  preprocessor = Age ~ ELOVL2_6,
  resamples = vfold_cv(X_ELOVL2_6, v = 5)
) %>% collect_metrics(summarize = TRUE)
```

The model seems OK-ish, but if you have some experience with linear models you may see something peculiar.

It becomes more apparent when you look at residuals (ie. error from the model):

```{r}
## plotting
ggplot( X_ELOVL2_6_a , aes( x = ELOVL2_6, y = .resid )) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_hline(yintercept=0 , linetype = 'dotted' ) + 
    geom_smooth() +
    ylab("residuals")
```

The pattern of residuals *may* be indicative of a higher order relationship between the marker and age.

But if that's the case, what is an appropriate degree for this model?

```{r}

X_ELOVL2_6_augmented = X_ELOVL2_6

for( degree in c(1,2,3,20)){

    R = recipe( X_ELOVL2_6 , Age ~ ELOVL2_6 ) %>%
                    step_poly( all_numeric_predictors(), degree = degree )

    wf = workflow() %>% 
        add_model( linear_reg( engine = 'lm' ) ) %>% 
        add_recipe( R ) %>% 
        fit( X_ELOVL2_6 )

    X_ELOVL2_6_augmented[ paste0("deg",degree) ] = predict( wf , X_ELOVL2_6 )$.pred
}

```

```{r}
ggplot( X_ELOVL2_6_augmented , aes( x = ELOVL2_6, y = Age ) ) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_line( aes(y=deg1), color = '#bfd3e6', linewidth = 1 ) + 
    geom_line( aes(y=deg2), color = '#8c96c6', linewidth = 1 ) +
    geom_line( aes(y=deg3), color = '#88419d', linewidth = 1 ) +
    geom_line( aes(y=deg20), color = '#4d004b', linewidth = 1 ) 
```

```{r}
for( degree in c(1,2,3,20)){
    R2 = rsq_vec( X_ELOVL2_6_augmented$Age , X_ELOVL2_6_augmented[,paste0('deg',degree)] )
    RMSE = rmse_vec( X_ELOVL2_6_augmented$Age , X_ELOVL2_6_augmented[,paste0('deg',degree)] )
    print(paste('degree',degree,' - R^2=',round(R2,3),' - RMSE=',round(RMSE,2)))
}    
```

-   which degree relationship is appropriate then ?
-   what of the other biomarkers ?

You guessed it, we come back again to hyper-parameters we have to evaluate in order to find the most appropriate model.

```{r}
R = recipe( X_ELOVL2_6 , Age ~ ELOVL2_6 ) %>%
                step_poly( all_numeric_predictors(), degree = tune() )

wf = workflow() %>% 
    add_model( linear_reg( engine = 'lm' ) ) %>% 
    add_recipe( R )


degree_res <- 
  wf %>% 
  tune_grid(
    resamples = vfold_cv(X_ELOVL2_6, v = 10),
    grid = grid_regular( list( degree = degree_int( range = c(1,10) )) , levels = 10)
    )

degree_metrics = degree_res %>% collect_metrics()

p1 = ggplot( degree_metrics %>% filter(.metric == 'rsq') , 
             aes( x = degree , y = mean ) ) + geom_line() + ylab( "R-square" )
p2 = ggplot( degree_metrics %>% filter(.metric == 'rmse') , 
             aes( x = degree , y = mean ) ) + geom_line() + ylab( "RMSE" )
grid.arrange(p1,p2,ncol=2)
```

So it seems that increasing power to 3 increases (at least a bit) our predictive power here.

But what about the other predictors?

## ML approach to linear regression - methylation data

As we add other predictors, it can be good to also add penalization terms.

We will also add the possibility of interaction between terms.

```{r}
R = recipe( df_meth , Age ~ . ) %>%
    step_normalize( all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
    step_poly( all_numeric_predictors(), degree = tune() )
    

wf = workflow() %>% 
    add_model( linear_reg( engine = 'glmnet', 
                           mixture = tune(),
                           penalty = tune() ) ) %>% 
    add_recipe( R )


degree_res <- 
  wf %>% 
  tune_grid(
    resamples = vfold_cv(df_meth, v = 10),
    grid = grid_regular( list( degree = degree_int( range = c(1,3) ),
                               mixture = mixture(),
                               penalty = penalty()
                               ) , levels = c(3,11,20) )
    )

degree_res %>% show_best(metric = 'rmse')
```

```{r}
best_model <- degree_res %>% select_best(metric = "rmse")
best_model
```

```{r}
final_wf <- wf %>% 
    finalize_workflow(best_model) %>%
    fit( df_meth )

df_meth_a = augment( final_wf , df_meth )
df_meth_test_a = augment( final_wf , df_meth_test )

print(paste( "train - R2=",
             rsq( df_meth_a , truth = Age , estimate = .pred  )$.estimate,
             " - RMSE=",
             rmse( df_meth_a , truth = Age , estimate = .pred  )$.estimate
))
print(paste( "test  - R2=",
             rsq( df_meth_test_a , truth = Age , estimate = .pred  )$.estimate,
             " - RMSE=",
             rmse( df_meth_test_a , truth = Age , estimate = .pred  )$.estimate
))
```

```{r}
ggplot( rbind( df_meth_a %>% mutate( data = 'train' ),
               df_meth_test_a %>% mutate( data = 'test' ) ),
        aes( x = Age , y = .pred , col = data ) ) + 
    geom_point( alpha = 0.8 ) + 
    ylab( "prediction" ) + 
    geom_abline( slope=1 , linetype='dashed')


```

```{r}
VI = final_wf %>% 
    extract_fit_parsnip() %>% 
    vi(sign = TRUE) %>%
    mutate(Variable = factor(Variable, levels = Variable))
VI %>% ggplot( aes(x=Importance, y=Variable, fill=Sign) ) +
    geom_col()
```

# KNN

You can also use the KNN algorithm for regression. Again you get the K nearest neighbors of the point you want to predict but this time instead of a vote it does a local average of the neighbors value (again weighted or not by their distance to your query point).

**micro-exercise:** complete the code below to train a KNN regressor model for the methylation data. Optimize the `n_neighbors` and `weights` hyper-parameters:

```{r}
R = recipe( df_meth , Age ~ . ) %>%
    step_normalize( all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
    step_poly( all_numeric_predictors(), degree = tune() )
    

wf = workflow() %>% 
    add_model( ... ) %>%  ## add model
    add_recipe( R )


degree_res <- 
  wf %>% 
  tune_grid(
    resamples = vfold_cv(df_meth, v = 10),
    grid = grid_regular( ... ) ## add grid
    )

degree_res %>% show_best(metric = 'rmse')
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

So we see that the model we get from KKN is not bad at all **but** the interpretability is lacking in this model.

> KNN regressor is not really good at predicting sparse neigborhoods (eg, the predictions for the extreme data points are not accurate).

## Random Forest

From the standpoint of tree, the only difference is that now, instead of the entropy or Gini criterion, **the decision which variable to use at any node is made using a regression metric**, such as squared error for example.

For example, consider this example, adapted from the sklearn website:

```{r}
# Create a random dataset
set.seed(1)
X = runif(80, min=0 , max=pi*2)
y = sin(X)*2
y[ 1:10 ] = y[ 1:10 ] + rnorm(10)*5 # additional noise on some points

train = data.frame(x=X,y=y)

ggplot( train , aes( x=x,y=y ) ) + geom_point()
```

```{r}
model1 = decision_tree(tree_depth = 2, cost_complexity = 0, mode = 'regression') %>% 
    fit( y~x , train )
model2 = decision_tree(tree_depth = 6, cost_complexity = 0, mode = 'regression') %>% 
    fit( y~x , train )

pred = data.frame( x = seq(0,pi*2,length.out=250) )
pred$pred1 = (model1 %>% predict( pred ))$.pred
pred$pred2 = (model2 %>% predict( pred ))$.pred

ggplot( train , aes( x=x,y=y ) ) + 
    geom_point( alpha = 0.5 ) + 
    geom_line( data = pred , aes( x = x, y = pred1 ) , color = 'cornflowerblue' ) +
    geom_line( data = pred , aes( x = x, y = pred2 ) , color = 'salmon' )
```

```{r}
tree_obj <- extract_fit_engine(model1)

rpart.plot(
  tree_obj,
  extra = 1
)
```

Of course with a single tree you do not get very far, unless the tree becomes absolutely huge.

But with a random forest you can aggregate the estimate from many trees to get somewhere nice.

```{r}
model3 = rand_forest(mode = 'regression') %>% 
    fit( y~x , train )

pred$pred3 = (model3 %>% predict( pred ))$.pred

ggplot( train , aes( x=x,y=y ) ) + 
    geom_point( alpha = 0.5 ) + 
    geom_line( data = pred , aes( x = x, y = pred1 ) , color = 'cornflowerblue' ) +
    geom_line( data = pred , aes( x = x, y = pred2 ) , color = 'salmon' ) + 
    geom_line( data = pred , aes( x = x, y = pred3 ) , color = 'chartreuse3' )
```

Let's try on the methylation data:

```{r}
R = recipe( df_meth , Age ~ . ) 

wf = workflow() %>% 
    add_model( rand_forest( mode = 'regression', 
                            min_n =  tune() 
                            ) ) %>% 
    add_recipe( R )

RF_res <- 
    wf %>% 
    tune_grid(
        resamples = vfold_cv(df_meth, v = 10),
        grid = grid_random( min_n( range = c(5,100) ),
                            size = 20 )
    )

RF_res %>% show_best(metric = 'rmse')
```

# Exercise

We go back to the potato dataset we introduced in notebook 3.

---

**Note**: here the data has already been filtered to keep only the top 200 genes (that is still a lot, but manageable ). However often your data will have >10 000 genes, which would create issues in practice (more that just slowing down the training, some models will fail to find a good solution).

solutions include:

 * detecting genes with low variance and removing them (you can use [step_rm](https://recipes.tidymodels.org/reference/step_rm.html) to remove variables by name once you have decided which to remove)
 * a preliminary PCA are your friend (use scores adapted to regression)

Anyhow, end of the rent. As I said in this dataset you should be OK (although you could try a PCA if you are curious)
